mcqs.question: Why does an immutable object require no synchronization to be shared safely across threads?
options: Because its state never changes after construction, so there's no write for a concurrent read to race against
Because immutable objects are automatically stored in a special thread-local memory region
Because the language runtime automatically wraps every field access in a lock for immutable classes
Because immutable objects can only be read by one thread at a time by definition
mcqs.explanation: No synchronization is needed because there is nothing to race on -- every field is set once and never changes, so concurrent reads can happen in any order with identical results. There's no special memory region or automatic locking involved, and immutable objects can absolutely be read by many threads at once -- that's the whole benefit.

mcqs.question: In the `Money` class example, why does `plus()` return a new `Money` instead of modifying `this.cents`?
options: Because a method named `plus` is forbidden from mutating any field
Because mutating `this.cents` would violate immutability -- any thread holding a reference to the original object would see it change
Because returning a new object is always faster than mutating an existing one
Because `cents` is a `long`, and `long` fields cannot be reassigned
mcqs.explanation: Mutating `this.cents` would break the immutability guarantee -- any other code holding that same `Money` reference would suddenly see a different value, reintroducing the exact shared-mutable-state problem immutability exists to avoid. There's no such naming restriction, allocation isn't always faster, and `long` fields can normally be reassigned -- the class simply chooses not to.

mcqs.question: A class has only `final` fields, including a `final List<String> tags`, and no setters. A caller does `obj.getTags().add("x")`. What is the correct diagnosis?
options: This is safe -- `final` fields cannot be mutated by any caller
This is only unsafe if `tags` is accessed from more than one thread simultaneously
This is unsafe -- `final` only fixes the reference, not the mutable list it points to, so the getter leaked a way to mutate internal state
This is safe because `List.add()` never mutates the underlying list
mcqs.explanation: `final` fixes the reference, not the referenced object -- if the getter returns the actual internal list, any caller can mutate it directly; that's the defensive-copy gap. This is a bug regardless of thread count (it breaks even the plain contract of immutability), and `List.add()` absolutely does mutate the list.

mcqs.question: Which fix correctly closes the 'final reference to a mutable object' leak for a `final List<String> tags` field?
options: Change `List<String>` to `ArrayList<String>` in the field declaration
Mark the `add` method of the returned list as `private`
Do nothing -- `final` collections are immutable by default
Defensively copy the list in the constructor and return an unmodifiable copy (or a fresh copy) from the getter
mcqs.explanation: The fix is to defensively copy on the way in and the way out, so no external reference can reach the real internal list. Swapping to `ArrayList` changes nothing about mutability; you can't selectively make a borrowed object's methods private; and `final` collections are not immutable by default in virtually any mainstream language.
